item.title: Best Buy sells Blu-rays online and in-store again
item.dc:creator: Scharon Harding
item.description: Popular titles like The Odyssey are being “sold & shipped by Best Buy."
item.content:encoded:
Best Buy is selling Blu-rays directly through its website and in physical stores again after exiting Blu-ray and DVD sales in 2023.

The Best Buy website’s movie section currently lists 15 Blu-rays (including one two-pack) that are “sold & shipped by Best Buy.” New titles available include The Odyssey (2026), Project Hail Mary (2026), Supergirl (2026), Super Mario Galaxy (2026), and Obsession (2025). Best Buy is also selling some older titles on Blu-ray, including It’s a Wonderful Life (1943), Saving Private Ryan (1998), and The Godfather (1972).

Most of the Blu-rays are available for purchase online and can be delivered to an address or picked up at a Best Buy store within a few days. As of this writing, The Odyssey appears to be in stock at Best Buy stores, as it’s currently listed as available for pickup within as little as an hour.

item.title: Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show
item.dc:creator: Ashley Belanger
item.description: Erratic Muse outputs sharing random bank, bitcoin balances aren’t real, Meta says.
item.content:encoded:
After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.

When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.

Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.

item.title: Trump admin orders Kalshi to halt wagers on what words Trump will say
item.dc:creator: Jon Brodkin
item.description: CFTC: Kalshi bets may violate US ban on contracts that can be easily manipulated.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration ordered prediction market Kalshi to stop offering event contracts that pay out based on whether President Trump will say a specific word before a particular date. Kalshi halted trading in the contracts while the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) conducts a review into whether the Trump mention contracts violate federal law.

CNBC reported yesterday that "Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of 'mention' contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC." Kalshi told media outlets that it is complying with the CFTC order.

The markets taken down by Kalshi allowed users to wager on whether Trump would say certain words, including nicknames and the names of countries and companies. A similar expired event contract that can still be viewed on Kalshi's website asked whether Trump would use the nicknames "Marjorie Traitor Greene," "Sleepy Joe," and "Whack Job" or "Wack Job" before April 2026.

item.title: The "shameful" measles data that lost the US its elimination status
item.dc:creator: Beth Mole
item.description: Measles became endemic in the US months ago—and it's only accelerating.
item.content:encoded:
International health authorities formally announced on Tuesday that the US has lost its measles elimination status, a hard-fought public health triumph won in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. The loss had been widely expected by public health experts for months, and the decision was leaked by the press last week. Still, having the designation officially stripped stings.

After the announcement Tuesday, public health experts, doctors, and political leaders decried the dramatic backslide for the US, calling it "shameful" and a "national embarrassment." News articles point to the staggering vertical rise of measles cases this year, currently over 5,400 cases, more than any other year since 1991. An explosive measles outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for over 1,500 of those cases. There have been 10 confirmed deaths across three states, several deaths just in the last week.

But the measles data that caused the US to lose its status—the bits of it that are public at least—paint a darker picture of where the US is in its rematch with measles, the most contagious virus known on Earth. For one thing, almost none of the data from this year—the cases, the explosive Pennsylvania outbreak, the deaths—factored in to the loss. It was lost earlier. What's happening now is a runaway epidemic.

item.title: Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories
item.dc:creator: Kyle Orland
item.description: With MyMems, Wright says he wants to "turn the simulation inward."
item.content:encoded:
The computer gaming world hasn't heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright's subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA. Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players' memories.

MyMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright's previous projects by "turn[ing] the simulation inward," as Wright's Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning. The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world.

“If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?" Wright says by way of example in the release. "If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?"

item.title: It shouldn’t be this easy to pedal 25 mph: Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo
item.dc:creator: Jacob May
item.description: This commuter bike will have you blazing through streets without any range anxiety.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve had only one experience of pedaling an e-bike after it ran out of juice, but it was enough to make checking the battery display an anxiety-driven habit: “Can I afford to use the highest assist level up this hill? Should I switch to eco mode to preserve power and make sure I have enough to get home with the bike lights on?”

These aren’t fun questions to have rattling around in your head while riding home in the dark.

But those intrusive thoughts never crossed my mind while I was testing Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo. I didn't experience range anxiety, even while blowing through city streets at 25-plus mph (40.2 kph). The bike has so much juice (840 watt-hours) and power (810 watts of peak power and 105 newton-meters of torque) from Specialized's 3.1 motor system that I could ride as far and as fast as I wanted without worrying about having enough battery to get back home.

item.title: Vulcan failure caused by inadequate fuel supply to engines, ULA says
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger
item.description: "ULA is a valued partner, and we look forward to Vulcan's return to flight."
item.content:encoded:
United Launch Alliance said Wednesday that the failure of its Vulcan rocket during a launch on Sunday was caused by inadequate fuel supply.

"ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday," the company said in a statement. "While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines."

The new information released by ULA confirms reporting from Ars Technica on Tuesday that the rocket's failure was not due to the performance of the vehicle's main engines, which are provided by Blue Origin.

item.title: Waymo has stopped its robotaxis from driving on the freeway—here’s why
item.dc:creator: Jonathan M. Gitlin
item.description: Robotaxis already had to be recalled in May after they entered highway construction zones.
item.content:encoded:
Waymo is currently restricting its fleet of robotaxis to surface streets after getting into hot water with California over its cars' driving behavior on highways. Specifically, the software tends to drive into construction zones at speed. As first reported by the San Francisco Business Times, this behavior actually drew the ire of California’s DMV earlier this month, which ordered Waymo to stop driving on Californian highways immediately and until it can convince the DMV that its cars no longer “pose an imminent hazard to public safety.”

This is not Waymo’s first run-in with this problem. In Arizona, Waymo robotaxis did not recognize ramp closure signs on six occasions in Phoenix in April and entered construction zones. A month later in California, seven Waymo robotaxis entered lanes with active construction. In June, Waymo recalled the almost 3,800 robotaxis capable of highway driving. That problem led Waymo to stick to surface streets only in California after the May incidents until late July, when the robotaxis resumed highway operations.

In early July, Waymo told the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration that it began updating the robotaxi software to a version that “improve[s] the recognition of freeway construction zones, more appropriately prioritize[s] construction zones over other freeway hazards, and reduce[s] speed when the AV detects that it may be in a construction zone.”

item.title: Tesla’s $30,000 Cybercab comes with a $299 monthly catch
item.dc:creator: Aarian Marshall, wired.com
item.description: Tesla can restrict where Cybercabs drive and even block owners from reselling them.
item.content:encoded:
There is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla’s self-driving Cybercab, several.

Last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet's Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox, offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks, but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s "limited release” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December.

From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.

item.title: Voyager 1 at one light-day: Historian revisits Golden Record's forgotten details
item.dc:creator: Robert Pearlman
item.description: "They are pretty confident that it's going to last a long, long, long time..."
item.content:encoded:
In the one light-day that humanity's most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again.

Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter's moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a "commemorative phonograph record," in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whoever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space.

About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson. While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs' overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago.

item.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review
item.dc:creator: Kyle Orland
item.description: Jason and Lucia's crime-heavy love story fuels a wonder of digital urban simulation.
item.content:encoded:
Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort.

This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI, a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple.

The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers.

item.title: Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it
item.dc:creator: Nick Indge
item.description: Word, Excel, and PowerPoint now live inside Copilot; always-on agents are next.
item.content:encoded:
Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company's vision for its new "frontier ecosystem," announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as "the new OS for work."

The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent's work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.

item.title: San Diego dumps both Flock cameras and smart streetlights
item.dc:creator: Cyrus Farivar
item.description: 500+ cameras will go dark just 3 years after mayor urged approval.
item.content:encoded:
On Monday evening, San Diego’s city council voted to end its contracts with two surveillance equipment vendors, Flock and Ubicquia. San Diego is one of the largest cities to end its relationship with Flock, the startup with an estimated valuation of $8.3 billion.

“We fucking won!” said Lilly Irani of the Transparent and Responsible Use of Surveillance Technology (TRUST) SD Coalition, speaking in her personal capacity.

She and her colleagues have been among the loudest critics in recent years.

item.title: Yet another satellite company is jockeying for a rocket—but this one makes sense
item.dc:creator: Stephen Clark
item.description: "Governments need control of their critical space infrastructure, and Europe needs it most."
item.content:encoded:
Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe's first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company.

The announcement came as an all-cash voluntary tender offer from an Italian subsidiary of ICEYE to Avio's shareholders, led by the Italian defense conglomerate Leonardo. Avio said its board of directors "has taken note of the notice" from ICEYE and is considering the purchase offer.

Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. The Vega C has flown successfully seven times in eight attempts since 2022. It is a follow-on to an earlier version of the Vega rocket that amassed a 20-for-22 record since debuting in 2012.

item.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
item.dc:creator: Dan Goodin
item.description: Malware cocktail delivers cryptocurrency theft payloads and iOS exploits, among other things.
item.content:encoded:
Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday.

ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword.

Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware

Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript.

item.title: “Trump was in bed with Jensen”: Critics balk at Huang’s wish to return to Nvidia
item.dc:creator: Ashley Belanger
item.description: “I love our country”: Jensen Huang’s apology comes amid escalating Nvidia probes.
item.content:encoded:
On Monday, large trucks began circling the streets of Washington, DC, carrying billboards urging Congress to investigate the Trump administration’s ties with Nvidia’s disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.

“Jensen was in bed with a spy from China,” the billboards created by the Tech Oversight Project (TOP) alleged. “Trump was in bed with Jensen.” TOP is a nonprofit that describes itself as “dedicated to reining in Big Tech.”

Currently, Trump is supporting a campaign to bring back Huang as Nvidia’s CEO—despite many Republicans calling it a “horrible idea." Breaking his silence, Huang issued a statement Tuesday saying he would be “honored” to return, but the board said reinstatement is not under consideration as an internal investigation into US spying claims remains ongoing. item.title: Civilization studio Firaxis Games lays off a third of staff
item.dc:creator: Samuel Axon
item.description: Studio head Heather Hazen is among those departing.
item.content:encoded:
Firaxis Games, the studio behind the Civilization and XCOM franchises of computer strategy games, last week laid off about a third of its staff, totaling around 60 people. That's according to a recent report in Bloomberg.

The report cites people "familiar with the cuts," saying that the flagship game the studio is currently working on, a new entry in the XCOM series, "has faced development struggles and missed a significant milestone." The departures also include the studio head, Heather Hazen.

item.title: Humanity braces for an alien invasion in 3 Body Problem S2 teaser
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Ouellette
item.description: “Wake up! They haven’t come 24 trillion miles to negotiate. They are coming to exterminate us.”
item.content:encoded:
You might be excused for forgetting about the existence of 3 Body Problem, Netflix's heady sci-fi series adapted from the award-winning novel The Three-Body Problem by Liu Cixin, the first book in his Remembrance of Earth’s Past trilogy. After all, it debuted in March 2024. But it was an exceptionally well-done, thematically rich series, and we're finally getting the second of a planned three seasons in January. Netflix just dropped the first teaser.

(Spoilers for S1 below.)

Created by David Benioff, D.B. Weiss (Game of Thrones), and Alexander Woo (True Blood), the first season followed two primary timelines. In the earlier one, a young Chinese astrophysicist, Ye Wenjie (Rosalind Chao), witnessed her father being beaten to death by Red Guards during the Cultural Revolution. Ye figured out a means of sending an interstellar message to possible extraterrestrial civilizations, receiving a response from a planet called Trisolaris.

item.title: OpenAI sued by California after admitting to 80 loss-of-control incidents
item.dc:creator: Jon Brodkin
item.description: AG: OpenAI tested dangerous AI without proper oversight and misled public about it.
item.content:encoded:
California sued OpenAI yesterday, alleging it has tried to evade responsibility for the Hugging Face attack and about 80 other incidents in which the company lost control of its AI. The lawsuit was filed under the state's public nuisance and unfair competition laws.

The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI's autonomous agents "may just be the tip of the iceberg," said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. "OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General’s Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing."

OpenAI had publicly reported only 27 such incidents, showing that "OpenAI’s public reports do not represent the full scope of loss-of-control incidents involving OpenAI’s models that have impacted third parties," the lawsuit said. OpenAI "knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it," Bonta said in a press release.

item.title: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger
item.description: Information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin.
item.content:encoded:
United Launch Alliance (ULA) confirmed Tuesday morning that its return-to-flight launch of the Vulcan rocket began failing during the initial stages of the mission.

"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff, the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," the company said.

The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight.
